rows.description: A teenager and a parent each remember an argument differently and both feel certain. Their memories are shaped by feelings and later thoughts.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A young adult is sure about a detail of a past event and is shown a photo or message proving otherwise. Confidence is not a measure of accuracy.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A mature person checks important facts against records, says I remember it this way, and lets others' memories be different without calling them liars.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A preschooler who is repeatedly asked about an event that did not happen may start to describe it. Imagination and memory blur easily at this age.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A child questioned with leading words by an adult or peers may adopt details that were never true. Neutral, open questions protect the accuracy of what he says.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager who hears friends recount a shared incident starts to remember events that only they described. Group talk can blend into personal memory.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A young adult recalls a detailed childhood scene that family members say never occurred. Vividness and emotion do not prove a memory is accurate.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.subtype: Careful with witness and family accounts [Response]
rows.description: A wise person avoids leading questions, records facts soon after events, and treats strong feelings about a memory as real without treating every detail as proof.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A preschooler says he saw a monster at the park when it was a story he heard. He knows the content but has lost track of where it came from.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A child mixes up something seen in a cartoon with something that happened at school and defends it sincerely. He is not lying, since the source tag is lost.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
